query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Annealing-induced modifications of the grain boundary structure in Q235 steel control the formation, continuity, and adherence of protective oxide scales by altering oxygen diffusion pathways, thereby determining the balance between corrosion protection and degradation under high-temperature aggressive salt conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 carbon steel (pre-exposure state) with its inherent microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject Q235 steel samples to controlled annealing treatments at approximately 800 °C in an air atmosphere for varying durations to achieve a range of grain sizes and grain boundary densities.
generation.conditions: Expose the annealed samples to aggressive salt environments (e.g., Na2SO4-60%V2O5 mixtures) at 700–900 °C. Additionally, conduct parallel corrosion tests under room-temperature salt exposure to delineate temperature-dependent effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Variation in grain boundary density and distribution that modulate the diffusion paths for oxygen, influencing nucleation and growth of the oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced grain boundary density in refined microstructures accelerates oxygen diffusion, promoting the formation of a continuous, adherent, and uniform protective oxide layer at high temperatures. In contrast, coarser-grained samples produce discontinuous oxide scales that may spall or allow further degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with an optimized, refined grain structure are expected to develop smoother, more uniform oxide scales with lower mass change and enhanced high-temperature corrosion resistance compared to untreated or coarser-grained Q235 steel. At room temperature, the protective mechanism should be less pronounced due to slower oxidation kinetics.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel in its as-received state featuring the original grain size and distribution.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to be dominant under high-temperature corrosive conditions (700–900 °C) with aggressive salt exposure. Under room-temperature conditions, the influence of grain boundary density on oxide formation is expected to be minimal due to slower diffusion rates.
generation.uncertainty: While the trend of improved oxide scale integrity with refined grain structures is expected, the exact quantitative relationship between grain boundary density and corrosion performance may be affected by other microstructural factors and impurities inherent in Q235 steel.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Q235 steel samples with a range of grain sizes generated by varying the annealing durations at 800 °C. Characterize the grain size and grain boundary density using microscopy techniques (e.g., EBSD). Expose these samples to a standardized hot-corrosion test (salt environment: Na2SO4-60%V2O5 at 700–900 °C), as well as to a room-temperature salt exposure test.
measurements: Grain size and grain boundary distributions (using EBSD or optical microscopy)
Mass change measurements after corrosion exposure
Oxide scale morphology, continuity, and composition (using SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no clear correlation is observed between enhanced grain boundary density and improved oxide scale uniformity or if samples with refined microstructures do not show reduced mass gain (or even perform worse) compared to the baseline material under hot-corrosion conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

proposals.material_system: Q235 carbon steel (in its as-received state)
proposals.intervention: Perform controlled pre-corrosion annealing treatments to modify the grain boundary character (e.g., grain size refinement vs. coarsening) prior to hot corrosion tests.
proposals.conditions: Anneal Q235 steel samples in controlled air atmospheres at ~800 °C for varying times to produce different grain sizes and then expose them to aggressive salt environments (e.g., Na2SO4-60%V2O5 mixtures) at 700–900 °C. A parallel room‐temperature salt exposure test should be conducted.
proposals.structural_mediator: Variation in grain boundary density and distribution controlling the nucleation and growth of protective (or deleterious) oxide scales.
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that annealing-induced grain structure modifications determine the oxidation kinetics: finer-grained microstructures offer more grain boundary area that can serve as rapid diffusion paths, promoting the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer that enhances corrosion protection at high temperatures; conversely, coarser grains might yield discontinuous layers, facilitating further degradation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated Q235 steel, samples with an optimized, refined grain structure will develop smoother, more uniform oxide scales with lower mass change and improved high-temperature corrosion resistance, while the coarser-grained baseline will show faster degradation. At room temperature, the differences may be less marked, indicating the mechanism predominantly applies under high-temperature conditions.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It isolates the effect of pre-exposure grain structure (a microstructural factor) on the development and protectiveness of oxide scales, thereby explaining why corrosion protection persists or fails across temperature regimes.

proposals.intervention: Introduce a controlled surface pre-treatment that enhances the distribution of minor alloying elements or impurities (such as Mn and Si) to promote preferential oxide formation.
proposals.conditions: Subject Q235 steel to a brief oxidative heat-treatment (e.g., 600 °C in low-oxygen partial pressure) to trigger selective surface segregation followed by salt exposure tests at high (700–900 °C) and ambient conditions.
proposals.structural_mediator: Segregation of impurity elements at the surface that act as nucleation centers for forming a mixed oxide layer.
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that intrinsic impurities in Q235 steel can segregate under controlled heat treatments to form a locally enriched zone which preferentially oxidizes, leading to a composite oxide that is more resistant to spallation and hot corrosion – a dynamic that may differ as a function of temperature regime.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated Q235 steel, the pre-treated samples will develop a more protective, slower-growing oxide layer during hot corrosion testing with lower mass change. Under ambient conditions, the effect is minimal, indicating the temperature-dependent activation of impurity segregation and oxide stabilization.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It directly tests a mechanistic hypothesis that impurity segregation controls oxide film formation and thus the persistence (or failure) of corrosion protection from room temperature to high temperature.

proposals.material_system: Q235 carbon steel with an applied HEA coating (e.g., FeCrMnNi system)
proposals.intervention: Deposit a thin high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating on Q235 steel using physical vapor deposition, then apply a post-deposition annealing treatment to promote interdiffusion and scale formation before corrosion testing.
proposals.conditions: After coating, anneal the samples at 800 °C in a controlled atmosphere for set durations to achieve compositional gradient formation, then subject the coated and interdiffused samples to salt exposures at 700–900 °C and room temperature.
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of an interdiffused interface and a modified surface oxide scale that is enriched in corrosion-resistant elements (from the HEA) compared to the base Q235 steel.
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that the HEA coating acts as a diffusion barrier and source of protective elements, altering the local oxidation kinetics so that a stable, adherent oxide scale forms. At high temperatures, this scale reduces mass change and corrosion, whereas at room temperature the underlying Q235 characteristics dominate.
proposals.predicted_outcome: In hot corrosion tests, the HEA-coated Q235 steel will exhibit lower mass gain and improved scale adherence relative to uncoated Q235 steel due to the formation of a more protective mixed-oxide layer, while under room-temperature exposure, the difference is less significant.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It tests whether modifications from an additional compositional layer (via HEA coating) can control the mechanism of oxide scale formation and thereby the persistence or failure of corrosion protection across different temperature regimes.

proposals.intervention: Apply pre-corrosion thermomechanical treatments to introduce controlled levels of residual stress (via cold working followed by partial annealing) and then evaluate the corrosion behavior.
proposals.conditions: Prepare Q235 steel samples with varying degrees of cold work (e.g., 10% vs. 30% thickness reduction) followed by a standardized annealing treatment at 700 °C to develop different residual stress profiles; then expose the samples to aggressive salt environments at 700–900 °C with simultaneous residual stress mapping and room-temperature tests as a control.
proposals.structural_mediator: Residual stress fields and defect densities (dislocations) that can serve as rapid diffusion paths for oxygen, thus affecting oxide nucleation and growth.
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that enhanced residual stress and higher dislocation density accelerate oxygen diffusion along defect channels, which may promote the rapid formation of a protective oxide if the oxidation front is well-controlled, or alternatively lead to brittle, defective scales if too high. This balance determines whether corrosion protection is retained or degrades.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples with moderate levels of residual stress (optimized via controlled cold work and annealing) will develop a uniformly adherent oxide scale with lower degradation rates under high-temperature hot corrosion compared to both the as-received and highly cold-worked (excessively stressed) samples. At room temperature, the influence of residual stress on the oxide formation mechanism will be reduced.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach isolates the role of mechanical history (residual stress) on oxide scale formation and subsequent protective behavior, providing a direct test of the role of defect-driven diffusion mechanisms in corrosion-related degradation or protection.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly tests the role of pre-exposure microstructure—in particular, the grain boundary density modified by annealing—in governing oxidation kinetics and oxide scale integrity. This approach isolates a key mechanistic factor that can explain why Q235 steel exhibits enhanced or compromised corrosion protection at high temperatures (700–900 °C) compared to room temperature. The hypothesis is clear, testable, and based on known diffusion phenomena, making it the most straightforward direction to address the research question.
